objectives: Read an attention heatmap and explain what each row/column means
Derive scaled dot-product attention from first principles
Explain why scores are divided by √d_k and what breaks without it
Tune d_k in a live sandbox and see the variance blow-up yourself

slides.title: Part 1 — Why attention exists
slides.body: The whole transformer is scaffolding around one operation. Before the mechanism, understand the *problem* it was invented to solve — then every design choice becomes inevitable rather than arbitrary.

slides.title: The sequential bottleneck of recurrence
slides.body:
For a decade, sequence models were **recurrent**. An RNN/LSTM consumes tokens one at a time, folding each into a fixed-size hidden state $h_t = f(h_{t-1}, x_t)$. Two structural problems follow directly from that recurrence relation, and both are fatal at scale.

**1. No parallelism along the sequence.** $h_t$ literally cannot be computed until $h_{t-1}$ exists. Training on a length-$n$ sequence is $n$ *serial* steps. GPUs are throughput machines with tens of thousands of ALUs; a serial dependency chain leaves them ~idle. Doubling sequence length doubles wall-clock time with no way to spend more hardware to fix it.

**2. Long-range signal decay.** To let token 1 influence token 500, information must survive 499 successive nonlinear updates. Backpropagating that far multiplies ~499 Jacobians; unless their norms sit in a razor-thin band the gradient vanishes (→0) or explodes (→∞). LSTMs' gating mitigates but does not remove this — empirically, dependencies beyond a few hundred tokens are weak.

> **Context:** Bahdanau et al. (2014) bolted an *attention* add-on onto an RNN translator so the decoder could look back at any encoder state. It worked so well that Vaswani et al. (2017), *"Attention Is All You Need,"* deleted the RNN entirely and kept only attention.

slides.title: Convolutions don't fix it either
slides.body:
A natural reaction: replace recurrence with 1-D **convolutions** (WaveNet, ByteNet). Convolutions *are* parallel across positions — good. But a convolution kernel of width $k$ only mixes information within a window of size $k$. To connect tokens $n$ apart you must stack $\mathcal{O}(n/k)$ layers (or use dilation, $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$). The path length between two positions still grows with distance, so the long-range learning problem is reduced but not eliminated, and depth balloons.

> **The requirement, stated precisely:** a layer that (a) is fully parallel across positions, and (b) connects *any two positions in a single step* (constant path length), so gradient between distant tokens doesn't have to survive many hops. Attention is the minimal construction satisfying both.

slides.title: Where attention sits in the transformer
slides.body: Orient yourself before the mechanism. A transformer block is exactly two sublayers: **attention**, then a **position-wise feed-forward network (FFN)**, each wrapped in LayerNorm + a residual connection. Of these, **attention is the only operation that moves information *between* token positions.** The FFN transforms each token independently; LayerNorm and residuals are stabilizers. So when people say "the model figured out that *it* refers to *the trophy*," the mechanism that did it is attention. Everything else in this path (FFN, norm, residual, positional encoding) exists to make a deep stack of attention layers trainable. Master attention and ~80% of the architecture is conceptual bookkeeping.

slides.title: Part 2 — Build the intuition before the math
Attention is a soft, learnable dictionary lookup
slides.body:
The cleanest mental model. A Python `dict` lookup: you present a **key**, get back its **value**, exact match only. Attention is the *soft, differentiable, content-addressed* generalization:

- Every token emits three vectors: a **query** $q$ ("what am I looking for?"), a **key** $k$ ("what do I contain?"), and a **value** $v$ ("what I'll contribute if selected").
- Instead of an exact key match, you score the query against **every** key, convert the scores to weights that sum to 1, and return the **weighted average of all values**.

A hard dict returns one value and has zero gradient (you can't differentiate "which key matched"). The softmax-weighted average is smooth: nudging a query slightly nudges the output slightly, so gradient descent can *learn* what each token should look for. "Soft" is not an approximation of the real thing — softness is the entire point, because it is what makes retrieval trainable.

slides.title: A concrete intuition: resolving a pronoun
slides.body: Sentence: *"The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because **it** was too big."* What does *it* refer to? Humans use world knowledge (big things don't fit in small things). A transformer must compute this. At the layer that resolves *it*, the **query** from *it* encodes "I am a pronoun seeking a concrete antecedent." The **keys** of *trophy* and *suitcase* encode "I am a candidate noun." The query·key score is higher for *trophy* (the configuration the model learned makes the sentence coherent), so *it*'s output vector becomes mostly *trophy*'s **value** — the pronoun is now contextually bound to the trophy. No rule was written; the Q/K/V projections that produce this were learned by gradient descent over billions of sentences. This single example previews everything: scores, softmax weighting, value mixing.

slides.title: Reading an attention heatmap
slides.body: This visualization is an $n\times n$ matrix: each **row** is one query token, each **column** one key token, brightness = attention weight (rows sum to 1). Look at the row for `are`: nearly all its weight sits on `cats` — the verb learned subject–verb agreement across intervening words. That pattern is *emergent*: nobody coded "verbs attend to their subject." It fell out of next-token prediction. Drag the controls: notice rows are distributions (one bright cell or a spread), and that different inputs induce different patterns. Spending real time reading these is the single best way to build attention intuition.

slides.title: Part 3 — Formalize it, step by step
The three projections Q, K, V
slides.body:
Let $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ be the stack of $n$ token embeddings (row $i$ = token $i$). Attention introduces exactly three learned weight matrices and applies them once:

$$Q = XW^Q,\qquad K = XW^K,\qquad V = XW^V$$

with $W^Q,W^K\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_k}$ and $W^V\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_v}$. So $Q,K\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_k}$ and $V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_v}$. Three facts to internalize:

1. $W^Q,W^K,W^V$ are the *only* parameters in attention — there is nothing else to learn here.
2. Q and K must share dimension $d_k$ because we will take dot products between them; V's dimension $d_v$ is independent (often $d_v=d_k$).
3. The *same* three matrices are applied to every token (weight sharing across positions) — that's what makes it parallel and parameter-efficient.

slides.title: Scores → weights → output
slides.body:
Given Q, K, V, the computation is three steps:

1. **Scores:** $S = QK^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$. Entry $S_{ij}=Q_i\cdot K_j$ is the raw affinity of query $i$ for key $j$ — large and positive when the two vectors point the same way.
2. **Weights:** scale by $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ (justified shortly) and apply **row-wise softmax**, so each row becomes a probability distribution over the $n$ keys.
3. **Output:** multiply by $V$: row $i$ of the result is $\sum_j A_{ij} V_j$ — a convex combination of *all* value vectors, weighted by relevance.

Put together: $;\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\text{softmax}\!\big(QK^{T}/\sqrt{d_k}\big)V.$ You will now reconstruct each design decision yourself rather than memorize this.

question.question: Derive scaled dot-product attention
question.goal: Starting from "each token should read a relevance-weighted blend of the others", reconstruct $\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$.

steps.prompt: We need a similarity score between query $Q_i$ and key $K_j$ that is cheap and rewards aligned directions. What operation?
steps.motivation: We need O(1) per pair, differentiable, and maximal when vectors point the same way — the dot product is the natural choice.
hints: It must be a single scalar per (i, j) pair.
It should grow when the two vectors align in direction and magnitude.
steps.reveal: The dot product $Q_i\cdot K_j$ is one cheap matmul for all pairs at once ($QK^{T}$) and is large exactly when query and key align.

steps.prompt: Raw scores are unbounded real numbers. We need non-negative weights that sum to 1 across keys. What turns a score vector into such weights?
steps.motivation: A convex combination of values requires weights ≥ 0 summing to 1; softmax is the smooth, differentiable map that does this.

options: ReLU then divide by the count

hints: Weights must be a probability distribution over the keys.
It must stay differentiable for backprop.
steps.reveal: Row-wise $\text{softmax}$ maps scores to a probability distribution over keys, so the output is a true weighted average of values.

steps.prompt: With d_k-dim unit-variance Q, K, the dot product variance is ≈ d_k. To keep softmax responsive, divide the scores by what?
steps.motivation: Variance ≈ d_k means std ≈ √d_k; dividing by √d_k renormalizes scores back to unit variance so softmax doesn't saturate.
hints: You want to divide by the standard deviation.
steps.reveal: Divide by $\sqrt{d_k}$: it rescales scores to unit variance, keeping softmax out of its saturated, zero-gradient regime.

steps.prompt: In one line, explain why we apply the weights to V (not to K or Q).
steps.motivation: Q and K only decide how much to attend; V is the payload — the information actually carried forward.

rubricCriteria.description: States V holds the information/content to be aggregated
Notes Q·K only determines the weights, not the content

hints: Think about which vector is the 'payload'.
steps.reveal: Q and K produce the weights; V is the content. The output is $\sum_j w_{ij} V_j$ — a relevance-weighted blend of value vectors.

question.explanation: You reconstructed every design decision: dot-product similarity, softmax for a convex weighting, √d_k for numerical stability, and V as the payload.

slides.title: Part 4 — A fully worked example, with shapes
Walk the shapes end to end
slides.body:
Concrete numbers beat symbols. Take $n=3$ tokens, model dim $d=8$, and $d_k=d_v=4$.

- $X$ is $3\times 8$. $W^Q,W^K,W^V$ are $8\times 4$.
- $Q=XW^Q,;K=XW^K,;V=XW^V$ are each $3\times 4$.
- $S=QK^{T}$ is $3\times 3$. Row 2 = $[\,Q_2\!\cdot\!K_1,;Q_2\!\cdot\!K_2,;Q_2\!\cdot\!K_3\,]$ — token 2's affinity to each key.
- Divide by $\sqrt{4}=2$; softmax each row → $A$, $3\times 3$, every row sums to 1.
- $AV$ is $(3\times 3)(3\times 4)=3\times 4$: each token replaced by a relevance-weighted blend of the 3 value vectors.

The output is $3\times 4$ — same number of tokens, possibly new feature dim. Crucially there is **no loop over positions**: all three tokens are processed by the same matmuls simultaneously. That is the parallelism recurrence could not give us.

slides.title: Numeric mini-example of one softmax row
slides.body: Suppose for query token 2 the scaled scores are $[2.0,;1.0,;0.0]$. Softmax: exponentiate $\to[e^{2},e^{1},e^{0}]=[7.39,2.72,1.00]$, sum $=11.11$, normalize $\to[0.665,;0.245,;0.090]$. So token 2's output $=0.665\,V_1+0.245\,V_2+0.090\,V_3$ — dominated by $V_1$ but not exclusively. Note how a score *gap* of 1.0 became a probability *ratio* of $e^{1}\!\approx\!2.7\times$: softmax turns additive score differences into multiplicative weight ratios. That property is why raw score scale matters so much — which is the next point.

slides.title: Why divide by √dₖ — the variance argument
slides.body: Model $Q_i,K_j$ as vectors of $d_k$ independent entries with mean 0, variance 1. Then $Q_i\!\cdot\!K_j=\sum_{m=1}^{d_k} Q_{im}K_{jm}$ is a sum of $d_k$ independent mean-0, variance-1 terms, so $\operatorname{Var}(Q_i\!\cdot\!K_j)\approx d_k$ and its standard deviation is $\approx\sqrt{d_k}$. For $d_k=64$ that's a std of **8** — scores routinely land at $\pm 16$. Softmax of widely separated logits is almost one-hot, and the gradient of a saturated softmax is ~0 *everywhere*, so the attention layer stops learning. Dividing scores by $\sqrt{d_k}$ rescales them back to unit variance, keeping softmax in its responsive (non-saturated) regime. It is a one-symbol constant with binary consequences for whether the model trains at all. You will watch this happen live in the sandbox.

question.question: Push d_k up. Find a setting where the *unscaled* score std stays ≤ 1.5 — you can't, which is the point.
question.harnessCode:
import numpy as np
np.random.seed(0)
dk = int(d_k)
Q = np.random.randn(64, dk)
K = np.random.randn(64, dk)
s = Q @ K.T
if scale >= 1:
    s = s / np.sqrt(dk)
metrics = {"score_std": float(s.std()), "d_k": float(dk)}
question.explanation: Unscaled, std grows like √d_k (≈8 at d_k=64) — softmax saturates. Flip scale=1 and std snaps back to ≈1 at any d_k. That single divisor decides whether the layer trains.

slides.title: What the sandbox showed (and why it matters in practice)
slides.body: Unscaled, score std grows like $\sqrt{d_k}$, softmax collapses to one-hot, gradients die — the loss flatlines from step 1. Flip scaling on and std snaps back to ~1 at any $d_k$. This is not a toy concern: it is *the* reason the $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ factor is in the formula and in every implementation. A surprising amount of "my transformer won't train" reduces to a missing or wrong scale factor (or, in decoders, a missing causal mask — next).

slides.title: Part 5 — Edge cases, pitfalls & the failures you'll hit
The two attention bugs you will actually write
slides.body:
In practice almost every broken attention layer is one of two bugs, both of which *look* fine and *compile* fine:

1. **Missing/incorrect $\sqrt{d_k}$ scaling** → saturated softmax → flat loss (just analyzed).
2. **Missing causal mask** in a decoder → during teacher-forced training each position can attend to *future* tokens (including the answer it must predict), so training loss looks great but generation is garbage, because at inference there is no future to peek at. Fix: add $-\infty$ to all scores $S_{ij}$ with $j>i$ *before* softmax, so future weights become exactly 0.

Both are silent: no exception, just a model that mysteriously won't learn or won't generate. Recognizing the symptom *is* the skill. Diagnose one:

question.question: Diagnose the failure.
question.scenario: A teammate ships an attention layer. Training loss plateaus immediately and never drops. You print the attention matrix: every row is almost perfectly one-hot from step 1. Q, K, V projections look fine.

rubricCriteria.description: Identifies missing/incorrect √d_k scaling (or otherwise over-large logits) as the cause
Explains saturated softmax → vanishing gradients → no learning
Proposes dividing scores by √d_k (or equivalent renormalization)

question.explanation: One-hot-from-step-1 + flat loss is the classic unscaled-logits signature. Variance ≈ d_k saturates softmax; its gradient is ~0 so nothing learns. Divide QKᵀ by √d_k.

slides.title: Other boundary conditions worth knowing
slides.body:
- **Padding masks:** batched sequences are padded to equal length; attention to pad positions must be masked ($-\infty$) or the model attends to garbage.
- **Numerical stability:** softmax is implemented with the max-subtraction trick (see the softmax lesson) so $e^{\text{large}}$ doesn't overflow — relevant because attention logits can still be moderately large.
- **Quadratic cost:** $S=QK^{T}$ is $n\times n$. Memory and compute are $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ in sequence length — the central scaling pain that FlashAttention and sparse/linear attention exist to address (covered in self-attention).
- **Rank/coverage:** a single softmax row can only express one weighting; representing several relations at once needs *multiple heads* (next lessons).

hints: Q is [n, d_k], K is [n, d_k].
slides.workedSolution: Q·Kᵀ multiplies [n, d_k] by [d_k, n] → an **[n, n]** matrix. Entry (i, j) = Qᵢ·Kⱼ, the raw similarity of query i to key j. After ÷√d_k and row-wise softmax it becomes the attention-weight matrix; times V gives the [n, d_v] output.

question.question: What does the matrix product Q · Kᵀ produce?
options: An n×n matrix where entry (i, j) is the similarity score between query i and key j
A scalar — the total attention magnitude
An n-dimensional probability vector over keys
A new embedding for each token in a different space
question.explanation: Q is [n, d_k] and K is [n, d_k], so Q · Kᵀ is [n, n]. Entry (i, j) is the dot product of query i with key j — a raw similarity. After ÷√d_k and softmax (row-wise) it becomes the attention-weight matrix.

slides.title: Heads specialize — a preview of interpretability
slides.body: Once trained, attention heads acquire recognizable, reproducible jobs: positional heads (attend to the previous token), syntactic heads (verb→subject), coreference heads (pronoun→antecedent), and the celebrated **induction heads** ("…A B … A → predict B") that underlie in-context learning. This visualization shows a coreference-like pattern. The reproducibility of these circuits is the empirical foundation of *mechanistic interpretability* — reverse-engineering trained networks. You're seeing the raw phenomenon that whole research agenda is built on.

Q/K decide the weights, V is the content
√d_k keeps the softmax from saturating so the layer can learn

slides.title: Where this goes — the rest of the path
slides.body:
You can now derive scaled dot-product attention from first principles, explain the $\sqrt{d_k}$ factor via the variance argument, and diagnose its two classic failure modes. The remaining lessons compose this primitive into a transformer:

- **Self-attention** — Q, K, V from the *same* sequence; $\mathcal{O}(1)$ path length vs. $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ cost; causal masking in depth.
- **Multi-head attention** — $h$ attentions in parallel subspaces so one layer expresses many relations at once; GQA for serving.
- **Positional encoding** — restoring order to a permutation-equivariant operation.
- **FFN, LayerNorm, residuals, the block** — the scaffolding that lets you stack attention 100 layers deep.

Everything important happens in attention; the rest is what makes a deep stack of it trainable.
